doc_description: The Coca-Cola Company Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2021 (NYSE: KO) details its shift to a networked global organization, reports $38.7B in revenue and $9.8B in net income, covers the BodyArmor acquisition, and provides extensive risk and legal disclosures—most notably an IRS transfer-pricing dispute with potential ~$13B exposure—alongside audited financials and controls.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: In this report, the terms “The Coca-Cola Company,” “Company,” “we,” “us” and “our” mean The Coca-Cola Company and all entities included in our consolidated financial statements.
structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements caution, noting risks, uncertainties, and no obligation to update.
- Company overview as a total beverage company with global reach (200+ countries), major categories, and leading brands (Coca-Cola, Sprite, Fanta, Diet Coke, Coca-Cola Zero Sugar); focus on consumer connection and daily execution.
- Purpose and strategy to drive net operating revenue and long-term value, anchored in three pillars: Loved Brands, Done Sustainably, For a Better Shared Future.
- 2021 organizational transformation to a networked global organization: regional operating units under four geographic segments, five global marketing category leadership teams, a corporate center, and a platform services organization.
- Operating segments: Europe, Middle East & Africa; Latin America; North America; Asia Pacific; Global Ventures; Bottling Investments; plus Corporate.
- Product and brand definitions (concentrates, syrups, fountain syrups, Company Trademark Beverages, Trademark Coca-Cola) and dual business model:
  - Concentrate operations (sell concentrates/syrups to bottlers; higher margins, lower revenues).
  - Finished product operations (sell finished beverages via consolidated bottlers/distributors and Costa retail; higher revenues, lower margins).
- Distribution system details, including unit case volumes (2021 vs. 2020), U.S. vs. non-U.S. mix, sparkling share, and key markets (Mexico, China, Brazil, India).
- Largest bottling partners (Coca-Cola FEMSA, CCEP, Coca-Cola Hellenic, Arca Continental, Swire) accounting for 41% of 2021 worldwide volume; bottlers are independent contractors.
- Bottler’s agreements:
  - Outside U.S.: fixed terms with termination triggers; often include nonexclusive fountain syrup rights.
  - U.S.: Comprehensive Beverage Agreements (CBAs), including expanding participating bottlers (EPBs) with exclusive territories, incidence-based pricing, governance, and performance requirements; participating bottlers with similar CBAs; legacy agreements remain for a small portion. Company supplies fountain syrups in the U.S.
  - Incidence-based concentrate pricing model broadly used.
- Promotional and marketing support to bottlers and customers totaled $4.7 billion in 2021.
- Bottling investment strategy: acquire underperforming or strategic bottlers to improve performance and later refranchise; use equity method for significant influence investments.
- Seasonality with higher sales in Q2 and Q3; weather can affect volumes.
- Competitive landscape: global, regional, and local competitors across nonalcoholic and alcoholic beverages; key competitors include PepsiCo, Nestlé, Keurig Dr Pepper, Danone, Suntory, Unilever, AB InBev, Kirin, Heineken, Diageo, Red Bull; competition on price, innovation, marketing, packaging, and channels; rise of e-commerce and private labels.
- Raw materials:
  - Water as a critical input and sustainability focus.
  - Sweeteners: HFCS (U.S.), sucrose (international), and non-nutritive sweeteners (aspartame, ACE-K, sucralose, etc.); procurement support via CCBSS.
  - Juice/juice concentrate (notably orange) with risks from greening disease and weather; key suppliers include Cutrale.
  - Coffee sourcing for Costa (Rainforest Alliance Certified, primarily Brazil, Vietnam, Colombia).
  - Packaging materials (PET, glass, aluminum, closures, fiber, labels, gases) sourced from multiple suppliers.
- Intellectual property: extensive patents, copyrights, trade secrets (including formulas), and trademarks; licensing to bottlers and third parties.
- Regulatory environment:
  - Compliance with broad U.S. and international laws (food safety, competition, labeling, environmental, data privacy).
  - California Proposition 65 considerations and positions on exemptions/compliance.
  - Container deposit, recycling, and stewardship regulations; environmental compliance expectations; growing complexity in data protection (GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, China, EU).
- Human capital management:
  - Board oversight of talent, culture, DEI, and executive compensation; succession planning.
  - Approximately 79,000 employees (2021), with union representation in some regions.
  - DEI commitments and metrics, including 2030 goals (50% women in leadership globally; U.S. workforce reflecting census across levels), pay equity analyses, and employee inclusion networks.
  - Compensation and benefits designed to attract/retain talent (base pay, incentives, equity, retirement, health, well-being, leave programs).
  - Culture and engagement driven by growth mindset; regular feedback and town halls.
  - Leadership, training, and development programs (Coca-Cola University, digital learning, Opportunity Marketplace, coaching/mentoring).
- Investor information availability via company website and SEC filings.
- Risk factors highlighted: COVID-19 pandemic impacts on demand (shift to at-home vs. away-from-home), supply chain disruptions, input cost pressures, and broader economic uncertainties; potential exacerbation of other risks.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: In addition to the other information set forth in this report, you should carefully consider the following factors, which could materially affect our business, financial condition and results of operations in future periods.
structure.summary:
- Employee development: Coca-Cola University; digital learning catalog (Harvard, eCornell, LinkedIn Learning); Opportunity Marketplace for project-based experiences; enterprise-wide coaching and mentoring programs.
- Investor information access: Company website hosts SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) and investor news; SEC filings also available via sec.gov.

- Item 1A. Risk Factors:
  - Risks related to operations:
    - Ongoing COVID-19 impacts on demand, channel mix, supply chain and costs.
    - Intense competition, pricing pressure, and need for strong marketing/innovation.
    - Innovation execution risk and IP considerations.
    - Shifts in retail landscape (consolidation, discounters, e-commerce) and channel conflict.
    - Challenges expanding in emerging/developing markets (infrastructure, talent, demand fit).
    - Potential negative consequences of productivity initiatives.
    - Talent attraction/retention and evolving workforce expectations.
    - Energy/fuel price increases or shortages affecting production/distribution.
    - Supply disruptions and cost inflation in ingredients, raw materials, packaging, and cans; reliance on limited suppliers.
    - General inflation and limited pricing power potentially hurting margins and volumes.
    - M&A and bottling acquisitions integration risks.
    - Dependence on third-party service providers and partners.
    - Labor relations, collective bargaining, and potential strikes/work stoppages.
  - Risks related to consumer demand:
    - Obesity and health concerns, sugar taxes, and stricter marketing/labeling rules.
    - Evolving preferences for health, transparency, sustainability, and digital shopping.
    - Product safety/quality risks and potential recalls.
    - Ingredient and packaging concerns (sweeteners, 4-MEI, BPA) and resulting regulation or litigation.
    - Execution risk in digitizing the Coca-Cola system.
    - Reputation/brand risks from negative publicity, activism, human rights, or sponsorship issues.
    - Macroeconomic and political instability, boycotts, sanctions, or trade restrictions.
    - New product launch risks, including entry into ready-to-drink alcohol and associated regulations.
  - Risks related to the Coca-Cola system:
    - Reliance on independent bottling partners and alignment on strategy, pricing, and innovation.
    - Bottlers’ financial health affecting Company revenues and equity income.
    - Refranchising and divestiture execution risks.
  - Regulatory and legal risks:
    - Changes in income tax laws/rates and significant ongoing IRS transfer-pricing litigation.
    - Increases in indirect taxes (excise, VAT, sugar-sweetened beverage taxes).
    - Container/packaging laws (deposits, recycling, recycled content, plastic restrictions) increasing costs.
    - Labeling/warning requirements (e.g., California Proposition 65) potentially inhibiting sales.
    - Litigation exposure across advertising, labeling, IP, tax, environmental, and employment matters.
    - Compliance risks in high-risk legal environments (anti-bribery/corruption, sanctions).
    - IP protection and potential disputes.
    - Broad regulatory compliance (competition, environment, plastics, water use, data privacy).
  - Finance, accounting and investment risks:
    - Foreign currency exchange volatility.
    - Interest rate exposure, LIBOR transition, and credit rating impacts.
    - Risk of not achieving long-term growth objectives.
    - Counterparty financial institution default risk.
    - Potential asset and investment impairment charges.
    - Dependence on realizing benefits from Monster strategic relationship.
  - Information technology and data privacy risks:
    - Cybersecurity incidents, system outages, third-party breaches, and business disruption.
    - Compliance with evolving global data privacy and localization laws; potential penalties and costs.
  - Environmental and social risks:
    - Achieving ESG goals amid stakeholder scrutiny; reporting and litigation risk.
    - Plastic packaging environmental impact, regulation, and consumer perception; cost and supply implications.
    - Water scarcity/quality affecting operations and reputation.
    - Agricultural commodity availability and sustainable sourcing challenges.
    - Climate change impacts on agriculture, water, operations, regulation, and consumer demand.
    - Weather variability impacting seasonal beverage sales.

- Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments: Not applicable.

structure.title: Unresolved Staff Comments
structure.heading: Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments
structure.start_phrase: Not applicable.
structure.summary:
- Environmental and regulatory concerns over plastic bottles and packaging could disrupt distribution and harm business results.
- Water scarcity and declining water quality pose significant risks to costs, production capacity, community relations, and reputation across the Coca-Cola system.
- Reliance on agricultural commodities (sugarcane, corn, sugar beets, citrus, coffee, tea) exposes the business to increased demand pressures, climate-related yield declines, regulatory changes, and potential supply and cost volatility.
- Climate change may reduce agricultural productivity, intensify water scarcity, disrupt supply chains and production through extreme weather, and increase compliance and energy costs due to new regulations.
- Failure to meet publicly stated sustainability and carbon-reduction goals could lead to negative publicity and reduced consumer preference.
- Short-term adverse weather (e.g., unusually cold or rainy summers) can temporarily depress product demand and sales.
- Disclosure note: “Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments—Not applicable.”

structure.title: Properties
structure.heading: Item 2. Properties
structure.start_phrase: Our worldwide headquarters is located on a 35-acre complex in Atlanta, Georgia.
structure.summary:
- Properties (Item 2): 
  - Headquarters: 35-acre complex in Atlanta, Georgia, comprising multiple office buildings for Corporate and North America staff, plus technical/engineering facilities and a reception center.
  - Global footprint: Owned or leased facilities worldwide for administration, manufacturing, processing, packaging, storage, warehousing, distribution, and retail.
  - Segment reporting: Properties are attributed to their geographic operating segments, except Costa retail stores (reported in Global Ventures) and consolidated bottling/distribution facilities (reported in Bottling Investments).
  - Facility summary as of December 31, 2021: 
    - 32 principal concentrate/syrup plants.
    - 93 owned and 7 leased beverage manufacturing/bottling plants.
    - 116 owned and 166 leased distribution/storage facilities.
    - 1,600 leased retail stores (predominantly Costa within Global Ventures).
    - Activity spans EMEA, Latin America, North America, Asia Pacific, Global Ventures, Bottling Investments, and Corporate.
  - Capacity/utilization: Management deems facilities suitable and adequately utilized, with flexibility to increase output via added personnel, equipment, additional shifts, or facility expansion; the Company regularly evaluates needs and may acquire/lease new sites or dispose of existing ones.

- Legal Proceedings (Item 3):
  - Overall: Aside from a referenced U.S. Federal Income Tax Dispute, management believes current legal matters are not expected to have a material adverse effect on the Company as a whole.
  - Aqua-Chem litigation:
    - On December 20, 2002, The Coca-Cola Company filed in Georgia seeking a declaration of no obligation for Aqua-Chem/Cleaver-Brooks liabilities; Aqua-Chem filed the same day in Wisconsin seeking a declaration that Coca-Cola is responsible for certain liabilities and alleging breach of contract (claimed costs exceeding $9 million). The Wisconsin case was stayed and later voluntarily dismissed without prejudice.
    - Background: Coca-Cola owned Aqua-Chem (1970–1981), purchased over $400 million in insurance covering certain product liability and other claims, then sold Aqua-Chem in 1981 to Lyonnaise American Holding, Inc. A 1981 stock sale agreement and a 1983 settlement agreement govern respective obligations for past/future claims. Cleaver-Brooks (an Aqua-Chem division) manufactured boilers.

structure.title: Legal Proceedings
structure.heading: Item 3. Legal Proceedings
structure.start_phrase: The Company is involved in various legal proceedings, including the proceedings specifically discussed below.
structure.summary:
- Properties (Item 2):
  - Headquarters: 35-acre complex in Atlanta, Georgia, housing corporate and North America segment offices, technical/engineering facilities, and a reception center.
  - Global footprint: Owned/leased facilities worldwide for administration, manufacturing, processing, packaging, storage, warehousing, distribution, and retail.
  - Segment reporting: Properties are reported by geographic operating segment, except Costa retail stores (Global Ventures) and consolidated bottling/distribution facilities (Bottling Investments).
  - Facility counts as of December 31, 2021:
    - Principal concentrate/syrup plants: 32 owned, 0 leased.
    - Principal beverage manufacturing/bottling plants: 93 owned, 7 leased.
    - Principal distribution and storage facilities: 116 owned, 166 leased.
    - Principal retail stores: 0 owned, 1,600 leased (primarily Costa in Global Ventures).
  - Management assessment: Facilities are suitable, adequately utilized with seasonal variability, and have room for additional capacity via staffing, equipment, shifts, or expansion; the Company may acquire/lease or dispose of facilities as needs evolve.

- Legal Proceedings (Item 3):
  - Overall: Aside from the U.S. Federal Income Tax Dispute, management does not expect pending legal matters to have a material adverse effect.
  - Aqua-Chem litigation:
    - Background: Former subsidiary (1970–1981); asbestos-related claims tied to Cleaver-Brooks boilers; ~15,000 active claims.
    - Actions: Dual lawsuits filed in Georgia and Wisconsin in 2002; Wisconsin coverage litigation (2004) determined insurers are jointly and severally liable up to policy limits; multiple insurer settlements reached.
    - Chartis insurers: Settlement repudiation led to new litigation; trial court and Wisconsin Court of Appeals rulings favored the Company/Aqua-Chem; Wisconsin Supreme Court denied review (2014).
    - Status: Georgia case remains stayed.
  - U.S. Federal Income Tax Dispute:
    - IRS Notice (Sept. 17, 2015): ~$3.3 billion additional tax for 2007–2009 based on transfer pricing; IRS reallocated >$9 billion of income to the U.S. parent, departing from a 1996 Closing Agreement methodology previously audited and accepted for 1996–2006.
    - Litigation: IRS designated the matter for litigation; Tax Court trial held in 2018. Tax Court Opinion (Nov. 18, 2020) largely favored IRS but allowed dividends previously paid by foreign licensees to offset royalties; Brazilian royalty issue reserved pending 3M case outcome.
    - Company position: Believes IRS/Tax Court misapplied regulations and that retroactive methodology change is unconstitutional; intends to appeal.
    - Reserves and potential exposure: Tax reserve recorded at $438 million in 2020; updated to $400 million as of Dec. 31, 2021. If the Tax Court methodology were ultimately upheld and applied to subsequent years, potential aggregate incremental tax and interest could be about $13 billion through 2021; ongoing application could raise the effective tax rate by ~3.5 percentage points. Upon final Tax Court decision and depending on outcomes, the Company estimates an initial payment of approximately $4.9 billion for 2007–2009 (as of Dec. 31, 2021), refundable in whole or part if it prevails on appeal.

- Mine Safety Disclosures (Item 4): Not applicable.

- Executive Officers (as of Feb. 22, 2022):
  - Manuel Arroyo, 54: Chief Marketing Officer since Jan. 2020; prior roles include President, Asia Pacific Group; President, Mexico BU; General Manager, Iberia; CEO of Deoleo, S.A.; senior roles at S.C. Johnson.
  - Henrique Braun, 53: President, Latin America operating unit since Jan. 2021; previously President, Brazil BU; President, Greater China & Korea BU.
  - Lisa Chang, 53: Senior Vice President and Chief People Officer since Mar. 2019; previously CHRO at AMB Group LLC and VP of HR for International at Equifax.

structure.title: Mine Safety Disclosures
structure.heading: Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures
structure.start_phrase: Not applicable.
structure.summary:
- Company updated its tax reserve to $400 million as of December 31, 2021, reflecting updated calculations and accrued interest.
- Ongoing dispute with the IRS and related Tax Court Opinion could result in significant additional liabilities for tax years 2007–2009 and potentially subsequent years, which may materially affect financial position, results of operations, and cash flows.
- If the Tax Court Methodology reallocating income from certain foreign licensees is upheld and applied to 2010–2021, the Company estimates an aggregate incremental tax and interest liability of about $13 billion as of December 31, 2021, with further accruals until paid.
- Continued application of the Tax Court Methodology is projected to increase the effective tax rate by approximately 3.5 percentage points annually under similar conditions.
- The Tax Court has not yet issued its opinion regarding Brazilian legal restrictions on royalty payments by the Company’s Brazilian licensee for 2007–2009; after issuance, the parties will determine the tax impact, followed by a final decision.
- Post-decision, the Company would have 90 days to appeal to the Eleventh Circuit and pay the tax and interest for 2007–2009; the estimated payment at that time is approximately $4.9 billion (including interest through December 31, 2021), with potential refunds if the Company prevails on appeal.
- Mine Safety Disclosures: Not applicable.

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: The following Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations (“MD&A”) is intended to help the reader understand The Coca-Cola Company, our operations and our present business environment.
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure
  - Item 6 omitted; Item 7 provides MD&A for The Coca‑Cola Company, intended to be read with audited financials.
  - MD&A sections: Business overview; Critical accounting policies/estimates; Operations Review (2021 vs. 2020); Liquidity, capital resources and financial position.

- Business model and operations
  - Total beverage company operating in 200+ countries; categories include Trademark Coca‑Cola, sparkling flavors, hydration/sports/coffee/tea, nutrition/juice/dairy/plant-based, and emerging beverages.
  - Two revenue streams: concentrate operations (higher margin, lower revenue) and finished product operations (lower margin, higher revenue).
  - 2021 revenue mix: 56% concentrate, 44% finished products; volume mix: 83% concentrate, 17% finished products.
  - Route to market via independent bottlers, distributors, retailers, and consolidated bottling operations (Bottling Investments segment); Costa retail included in Global Ventures.

- Business environment and COVID‑19
  - 2021 still impacted by COVID‑19 (variant waves, supply chain and labor constraints, inflation), but recovery vs. 2020 as away‑from‑home channels reopened and vaccinations progressed.
  - Continued priorities: employee safety, supply continuity, product quality, channel support.
  - Transformation into a networked global organization; focus on portfolio prioritization, scalable innovation, consumer‑centric marketing, data‑driven revenue growth management, and embedding ESG goals.

- Key challenges and risks highlighted

  - Pension plans: discount rate and expected return assumptions; 2021 net periodic pension income and 2022 outlook sensitivity.
  - Revenue recognition: transfer of control; incidence‑based concentrate pricing; variable consideration estimation.
  - Income taxes: uncertain tax positions, deferred tax assets/liabilities, indefinite reinvestment of foreign earnings.

- Operations Review highlights (2021 vs. 2020)
  - Volume:
    - Worldwide unit case volume +8%; concentrate sales volume +9%.
    - Regional unit case growth: EMEA +9%, Latin America +6%, North America +5%, Asia Pacific +10%, Global Ventures +17%, Bottling Investments +11%.
    - Recovery led by away‑from‑home channels; strong growth in key markets (e.g., India +33% unit cases).
  - Net operating revenues
    - Up 17% to $38.7B; drivers: volume (+9%), price/product/geographic mix (+6%), FX (+1%); acquisitions/divestitures neutral overall.
    - Mix improvement from channel/package normalization post‑2020 lockdowns; pricing actions in Latin America and North America.
  - Profitability
    - Gross margin up to 60.3% (pricing/mix and channel recovery), partially offset by higher commodity and transportation costs (expected to continue rising in 2022).
    - SG&A up 25% to $12.1B (higher incentive/stock‑based comp, increased marketing vs. 2020 pullback, higher donations; FX +2%).
    - Other operating charges $846M (fairlife contingent consideration remeasurement; strategic realignment; BodyArmor transaction/transition costs; productivity program; trademark impairments).
    - Operating income up 15% to $10.3B; operating margin 26.7% (vs. 27.3%); FX +2% on operating income.
    - Regional operating income drivers: broad-based volume growth, favorable mix and pricing; Global Ventures swung to profit with Costa reopening.
  - Non‑operating items
    - Interest income down; interest expense up (higher debt extinguishment charges).
    - Equity income up 47% to $1.44B (better bottler performance, FX).
    - Other income (loss) — net: $2.0B income, including gains on BodyArmor step‑up, sale of Coca‑Cola Amatil stake to CCEP, securities gains; offset by U.S. manufacturing restructuring and pension settlement costs; modest net FX losses.
  - Taxes
    - Effective tax rate 21.1% (drivers include jurisdictional mix, equity income, stock comp, discrete items; tax incentives in several countries).
    - Ongoing transfer pricing litigation with IRS (Tax Court Opinion largely adverse in 2020; Company disagrees and will appeal); disclosure of potential maximum aggregate tax/interest exposure if IRS method applied through 2021.

- Liquidity, capital resources, and financial position
  - Strong operating cash flow ($12.6B, up 28%); working capital initiatives include supply chain finance and receivables factoring programs.
  - Cash, cash equivalents, short‑term investments and marketable securities of $12.6B; $8.1B in available backup credit lines; ongoing access to commercial paper and long‑term debt markets.
  - 2021 financing: ~$6.0B USD and €3.2B euro long‑term notes issued; significant long‑term debt extinguishments.
  - Capital allocation priorities: invest in the business, grow dividend (60th consecutive annual increase approved for 2022), disciplined M&A, resume share repurchases (~$500M expected in 2022 plus offset of SBC issuances).
  - 2021 investing: BodyArmor acquisition; CCA stake sale; capex $1.37B (largest in Bottling Investments and Global Ventures).
  - 2021 financing: net cash used $6.8B; no buybacks under board authorizations; dividends paid $7.25B.
  - Contractual obligations presented (debt and interest, taxes, purchase/marketing/lease/acquisition obligations); pension funding outlook and self‑insurance reserves disclosed.

- Foreign exchange and inflation
  - 2021 FX tailwind: +1% to revenue, +2% to income before taxes; detailed currency movements and hedging program; modest net FX losses in other income (loss).
  - Inflation expected to be mitigated over time through pricing; commodity and transportation cost pressures highlighted for 2022.

- Item 7A: Market risk and risk management
  - Use of derivatives to hedge FX, interest rate, commodity, and other risks; no trading for speculation.
  - FX: notional $13.7B; hedge accounting positions in net unrealized gain; sensitivity to USD weakening.
  - Interest rates: active mix management of fixed/variable and tenor; 1 pp rate increase sensitivity (~$125M higher interest expense, partially offset by higher interest income).
  - LIBOR transition addressed with amendments and alternative reference rates.

structure.start_phrase:

and other market risks.
structure.summary:

- Outlines market risk framework (Item 7A): use of derivatives solely for hedging (not trading) across foreign exchange, interest rates, and commodities; reliance on high correlation to offset underlying exposures; monitoring via sensitivity analyses; additional details in Note 5.
- Foreign exchange risk: managed on a consolidated basis leveraging natural offsets across 70 functional currencies; $25.6 billion of 2021 net operating revenues generated outside the U.S. Hedging tools include forwards, options, collars, and net investment hedges. FX derivative notional values were $13,691 million (2021) vs. $16,663 million (2020). Hedge-accounting FX derivatives had a net unrealized gain of $174 million as of 12/31/21; a 10% U.S. dollar weakening would reduce it to $172 million. Non-hedge-accounting FX derivatives had a $10 million net unrealized gain; a 10% U.S. dollar weakening would increase fair value by $58 million.
- Interest rate risk: exposure managed via mix of fixed/variable and term, with interest rate swaps used as needed. A 1 percentage point rate increase would have raised 2021 interest expense by $125 million, partially offset by higher interest income. Investment portfolio (highly liquid, investment-grade debt managed under policy limits) would see a $52 million fair value decline from a 1 percentage point rate increase.
- Commodity price risk: exposures include sweeteners, metals, juices, PET, and fuels; managed primarily via supplier pricing agreements and, when appropriate, derivatives (some not qualifying for hedge accounting but effective as economic hedges). Commodity derivative notional values were $918 million (2021) vs. $726 million (2020). No significant hedge-accounting commodity derivatives at 12/31/21; non-hedge-accounting derivatives had a $127 million net gain; a 10% commodity price decrease would reduce fair value by $71 million.

nodes.start_phrase: The accompanying consolidated financial statements have been prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States (“U.S. GAAP”).
nodes.summary:
- Document section: Note 1 to The Coca-Cola Company’s consolidated financial statements—Business and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies.
- Description of business: Coca-Cola is a total beverage company with brands grouped into Trademark Coca-Cola; sparkling flavors; hydration, sports, coffee and tea; nutrition, juice, dairy and plant-based; and emerging beverages. Owns/markets five of the world’s top six nonalcoholic sparkling soft drink brands (Coca-Cola, Sprite, Fanta, Diet Coke, Coca-Cola Zero Sugar). Products sold in 200+ countries/territories via a global network of independent bottlers, distributors, wholesalers, retailers, and Company-owned bottling/distribution; Coca-Cola beverages account for 2.1 billion of ~63 billion daily beverage servings worldwide.
- Basis of presentation: Financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP. Preparation requires estimates and assumptions affecting assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses, and contingencies; actual results may differ. Future impairment testing outcomes may change with different assumptions or conditions.
- Principles of consolidation: Consolidates entities controlled via majority voting interest and consolidates VIEs when the Company is the primary beneficiary (power to direct significant activities and exposure to significant benefits/losses).
- VIE involvement:
  - VIEs where Coca-Cola is not the primary beneficiary (primarily bottling operations): interests via equity investments, profit guarantees, or subordinated financial support; maximum exposure to loss was $1,980 million at December 31, 2021 and $2,567 million at December 31, 2020; individually not significant to consolidated financials.
  - VIEs where Coca-Cola is the primary beneficiary (also primarily bottling operations): consolidated; maximum exposure to loss was $103 million at December 31, 2021 and $74 million at December 31, 2020; assets and liabilities not significant to consolidated financials.
  - Creditors of VIEs have no recourse to the general credit of the Company.

nodes.title: Principles of Consolidation
nodes.heading: Principles of Consolidation
nodes.start_phrase: Our Company consolidates all entities that we control by ownership of a majority voting interest.
nodes.summary:
- Document context: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements — Note 1: Business and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies for The Coca-Cola Company and subsidiaries.

- Business overview:
  - Total beverage company with brands grouped into: Trademark Coca-Cola; sparkling flavors; hydration/sports/coffee/tea; nutrition/juice/dairy/plant-based; and emerging beverages.
  - Owns five of the world’s top six nonalcoholic sparkling soft drink brands (Coca-Cola, Sprite, Fanta, Diet Coke, Coca-Cola Zero Sugar).
  - Products sold in 200+ countries/territories via a global system of independent bottlers, distributors, wholesalers, retailers, and Company-owned bottling/distribution.
  - Beverages bearing Company trademarks represent 2.1 billion of ~63 billion daily beverage servings worldwide.

- Basis of presentation:
  - Prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP.
  - Use of estimates and assumptions that affect reported amounts and disclosures; actual results may differ. Future impairment outcomes may change with different assumptions/conditions.

- Principles of consolidation:
  - Consolidates entities controlled via majority voting interest; also consolidates certain entities under variable interest entity (VIE) guidance when the Company is the primary beneficiary (power + economics).
  - VIE interests primarily in bottling operations.
  - Not primary beneficiary: maximum exposure to loss of $1,980 million (2021) and $2,567 million (2020); not individually significant to consolidated financials.
  - Primary beneficiary (consolidated VIEs): maximum exposure to loss of $103 million (2021) and $74 million (2020); assets/liabilities not significant to consolidated financials.
  - Creditors of VIEs have no recourse to the general credit of the Company.

- Equity method investments:
  - Applied when the Company has significant influence; includes share of investees’ net income/loss.
  - Influence assessed via ownership, board representation, policy participation, commercial arrangements, and intercompany transactions.
  - Eliminates significant intercompany transactions, including with consolidated VIEs and equity method investees.

- Revenue recognition:
  - Recognizes revenue upon satisfaction of performance obligations, generally the sale of concentrates, syrups, or finished products to bottlers, wholesalers, distributors, or retailers (referenced Note 3).

- Advertising costs:
  - Production costs expensed upon first run; other marketing expensed as incurred.
  - Advertising expense: $4 billion (2021), $3 billion (2020), $4 billion (2019).
  - Prepaid advertising/production: $57 million (2021) and $83 million (2020).

- Shipping and handling:
  - Costs from manufacturing to distribution centers included in cost of goods sold (COGS).
  - Costs from manufacturing/distribution centers to customers also in COGS, except consolidated bottlers’ distribution costs, which are in SG&A.
  - Treats post-control shipping/handling as fulfillment costs; accrues related costs if revenue recognized before shipment.

- Sales, use, value-added, and excise taxes:
  - Taxes collected on behalf of customers are excluded from net operating revenues and recorded in receivables/payables until remitted.
  - Taxes imposed directly on the Company (e.g., based on sales, procurement, manufacturing) recorded in COGS.

- Net income per share:
  - Basic EPS: net income attributable to shareowners divided by weighted-average shares outstanding.
  - Diluted EPS includes effect of dilutive securities; approximately 6 million stock options antidilutive and excluded in 2021 and 2020; 2019 exclusion insignificant.

- Cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash:
  - Instruments with original maturities of three months or less classified as cash equivalents or restricted cash equivalents.
  - Restricted cash/equivalents generally include amounts held by captive insurance companies.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition
nodes.heading: Revenue Recognition
nodes.start_phrase: Our Company recognizes revenue when performance obligations under the terms of the contracts with our customers are satisfied.
nodes.summary:
- Equity method accounting: Investments with significant influence are accounted for under the equity method, with the Company’s proportionate share of investees’ net income/loss included in consolidated results. Significant influence is assessed via ownership, board representation, policy-making participation, commercial arrangements, and intercompany transactions. All significant intercompany transactions are eliminated, including with consolidated VIEs and the intercompany portions with equity method investees.
- Revenue recognition: Revenue is recognized when performance obligations are satisfied, typically the sale of concentrates, syrups, or finished products to bottlers, wholesalers, distributors, or retailers (see Note 3).
- Advertising costs: Production costs of ads are expensed at first run; other marketing is expensed as incurred. Advertising expense was $4B (2021), $3B (2020), and $4B (2019). Advertising and production costs recorded as prepaid were $57M (2021) and $83M (2020).
- Shipping and handling: Costs from manufacturing to distribution centers and to customers are included in cost of goods sold, except distribution by consolidated bottlers to customers, which is in SG&A. Customers generally do not pay separately for these costs. The Company treats post-control shipping/handling as fulfillment costs and accrues related costs if revenue is recognized before shipment.
- Sales, use, VAT, and excise taxes: Taxes collected from customers and remitted to authorities are excluded from net operating revenues and presented as receivables/payables until remitted. Taxes imposed directly on the Company (e.g., on sales, procurement, or manufacturing) are recorded in cost of goods sold.
- Net income per share: Basic EPS uses weighted-average shares; diluted EPS includes dilutive securities where applicable. Approximately 6 million stock options were antidilutive and excluded in both 2021 and 2020; exclusions in 2019 were insignificant.
- Cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash: Time deposits and highly liquid investments with maturities of three months or less are classified as cash equivalents or restricted cash equivalents. Restricted amounts generally relate to funds held by captive insurance companies.

nodes.title: Short-Term Investments
nodes.heading: Short-Term Investments
nodes.start_phrase: We classify time deposits and other investments that have maturities of greater than three months but less than one year as short-term investments.
nodes.summary:

- Debt securities: classified as held-to-maturity (amortized cost) when there is positive intent and ability to hold; otherwise carried at fair value and classified as trading or available-for-sale.

  - Expense recognition: straight-line over service period; recognize when minimum performance becomes probable (including catch-up for elapsed service); reverse expense if threshold no longer probable. Company estimates forfeitures and trues up at vesting.

Variable consideration is estimated and constrained to avoid significant reversals, based on assumptions about customer sales volumes, ending inventories, selling prices per unit, channels, and discounts/rebates. Estimates are typically developed using a portfolio approach at the country and product line level and affect trade accounts receivable and accounts payable/accrued expenses. Public investments use market quotes; nonpublic valuations may use discounted cash flows, estimated sale proceeds, or appraisals. nodes.title: HEDGING TRANSACTIONS AND DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS
nodes.heading: NOTE 5: HEDGING TRANSACTIONS AND DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS
nodes.start_phrase: The Company is directly and indirectly affected by changes in certain market conditions.

Related solvency capital funds held in securities totaled $1,670 million (2021) and $1,389 million (2020), classified as other noncurrent assets and not available for current obligations.
- Hedging and derivatives objective: Manage market risks—foreign currency exchange, commodity prices, and interest rates—using derivatives (forwards, futures, options, collars, swaps) and certain non-derivative instruments (e.g., foreign currency debt). No derivatives used for trading.
- Accounting and presentation: All derivatives carried at fair value in specified balance sheet line items, reflecting master netting and cash collateral where applicable. Hedge accounting applied when designated and qualified:
  - Fair value hedges: changes recognized in earnings in the same line as the hedged item.
  - Cash flow and net investment hedges: changes recorded in AOCI and reclassified to earnings when hedged items affect income.
  - Undesignated derivatives: changes recognized immediately in earnings.
  Formal hedge designation, documentation, and effectiveness testing at inception and quarterly. Fair values based on quoted prices or models; notional amounts are not measures of risk exposure. Instruments are OTC with liquid markets.
- Adoption of ASU 2017-12 (effective Jan 1, 2019): For cash flow hedges, entire change in hedge fair value recorded in OCI; no components excluded from effectiveness tests. Adoption effects included a $6 million net increase to reinvested earnings (with a corresponding AOCI decrease). For fair value hedges of interest rate risk, elected benchmark rate component method; recorded a $24 million increase to hedged long-term debt and an $18 million net-of-tax decrease to reinvested earnings.

- Fair value of non-designated derivatives (Dec 31): Assets totaled $196 million (2021) vs $137 million (2020); liabilities totaled $50 million (2021) vs $57 million (2020). Instruments include foreign currency, commodity, and other derivatives, with current and noncurrent classifications; gross disclosures referenced to Note 16.
- Counterparty credit risk: Transactions only with investment-grade financial institutions; ongoing monitoring and collateral provisions upon downgrades; stricter standards for longer-dated instruments; master netting and counterparty diversification reduce risk. Counterparty default risk considered minimal.
- Cash flow hedging strategy: Hedges variability in cash flows from FX, commodities, and interest rates; effective portions recognized in AOCI and reclassified when earnings are affected; ineffective portions go to earnings. Typical hedge horizon up to three years. Foreign currency cash flow hedging program (primarily EUR, GBP, JPY) uses forwards, options, and collars to hedge USD-denominated inflows/outflows; describes offsetting effects of USD strength/weakness. - Economic (non-designated) hedges:
  - General: Used as economic hedges of FX, interest rate, and commodity risks; changes in fair value recognized immediately in earnings.

- Scope: The Company sponsors/contributes to U.S. pension and postretirement health and life plans covering substantially all U.S. employees, plus nonqualified, unfunded defined benefit (DB) plans for certain employees and various plans outside the U.S.
- Primary U.S. plan: The funded DB plan not tied to collective bargaining; at December 31, 2021 it represented 61% of consolidated projected benefit obligation (PBO) and 57% of pension plan assets.
- Obligations and assets (2021 vs. 2020):
  - Pension plans: PBO fell to $8.58 billion (from $9.41b); assets rose to $8.91 billion (from $8.64b); net recognized position improved to a $325 million asset (from a $775 million liability).
  - Other postretirement benefit (OPEB) plans: Accumulated postretirement benefit obligation decreased to $696 million (from $769m); assets increased to $419 million (from $396m); net liability improved to $277 million (from $373m).
  - Pension accumulated benefit obligation (ABO): $8.43 billion (2021) vs. $9.26 billion (2020).
- 2021 key activity drivers:
  - Costs: Service cost $97m (pensions), $9m (OPEB); interest cost $183m (pensions), $15m (OPEB).
  - Returns and contributions: Actual return on assets $1,003m (pensions), $15m (OPEB); employer contributions $33m (pensions); participant contributions $6m (pensions) and $8m (OPEB).
  - Cash flows/events: Benefits paid $375m (pensions) and $67m (OPEB); pension settlements $491m; FX translation losses reduced obligations/assets.
- Actuarial gains/losses and assumptions:
  - Discount rate changes were the primary driver: an increase in 2021 generated a $197m actuarial gain in the primary U.S. pension plan; a decrease in 2020 produced a $491m loss.
  - Other factors: assumption updates, plan experience, and impacts from strategic realignment.
- Plan changes and restructuring:
  - 2021 OPEB amendment reduced obligations by $13m.
  - Settlements and curtailments in both years were primarily linked to strategic realignment initiatives.

nodes.title: Investment Strategy for U.S. Pension Plans
nodes.heading: Investment Strategy for U.S. Pension Plans
nodes.start_phrase: The Company utilizes the services of investment managers to actively manage the assets of our U.S. pension plans.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of investment strategy for U.S. pension plans, including use of external managers, asset allocation targets, and governance via investment guidelines.
- Long-term objectives: optimize returns at acceptable risk, maintain broad diversification across asset classes and managers, and control risk within each asset class.
- Target U.S. asset allocation: 42% equities, 30% fixed income, 28% alternatives.
- Equity breakdown: 60% global, 16% emerging markets, 24% U.S. small/mid-cap; company stock ~5% of global equities (~3% of total plan assets); emphasis on diversification and recognition of higher volatility in EM and small/mid-cap.
- Fixed-income breakdown: 33% long-duration high-quality bonds (diversified for duration/credit), 67% multi-strategy alternative credit (high-yield, bank loans, structured credit, EM debt) to enhance returns and diversify fixed income.
- Alternatives (28%): hedge funds, reinsurance, private equity, LBOs, international venture capital, and real estate; targeted for higher returns, with acknowledgment of illiquidity and long-term evaluation.
- Manager oversight: defined guidelines on eligible securities, diversification, and credit quality; written approval required for deviations; no manager >8% of U.S. plan assets as of Dec 31, 2021.
- Investment strategy for non-U.S. pension plans: for 70% of international plans (mainly Europe/Canada) long-term target of 66% equities, 4% fixed income, 30% other; remaining 30% had actual allocation of 44% mutual/pooled/commingled funds, 21% fixed income, 1% equities, 34% other.
- Note that international strategies vary by plan and local laws; no single non-U.S. plan is individually material.

nodes.title: Investment Strategy for Non-U.S. Pension Plans
nodes.heading: Investment Strategy for Non-U.S. Pension Plans
nodes.start_phrase: The long-term target allocation for 70 percent of our international subsidiaries’ pension plan assets, primarily certain of our European and Canadian plans, was 66 percent equity securities, 4 percent fixed-income securities and 30 percent other investments.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines investment strategy for U.S. pension plans managed by external investment managers under defined guidelines and asset allocation targets aimed at long-term obligations.
- Target U.S. asset mix: 42% equities, 30% fixed income, 28% alternatives, designed to optimize returns at acceptable risk, ensure broad diversification across asset classes and managers, and control risk within each class.
- Manager guidelines specify eligible/ineligible securities, diversification, and credit quality; deviations require written approval; no single manager held more than 8% of assets as of December 31, 2021.
- Equity allocation (42%) breakdown: 60% global equities, 16% emerging markets, 24% U.S. small/mid-cap; global equity returns driven by security, country, and sector diversification; company stock ~5% of global equities and ~3% of total plan assets; EM and small/mid-cap targeted for capital appreciation despite higher volatility.
- Fixed income allocation (30%) breakdown: 33% long-duration bonds (high-quality, diversified to manage duration/credit risk) and 67% multi-strategy alternative credit (high yield, bank loans, structured credit, EM debt) to enhance returns and diversify fixed income exposure.
- Alternative investments (28%): hedge funds, reinsurance, private equity, LBO funds, international venture capital, and real estate; intended to outperform public equities; characterized by illiquidity and long-term horizons.
- Describes non-U.S. pension plan strategies: for 70% of international plans (mainly Europe/Canada), long-term target is 66% equities, 4% fixed income, 30% other; the remaining 30% of assets were actually allocated 44% to mutual/pooled/commingled funds, 21% fixed income, 1% equities, 34% other.
- Notes that international strategies vary by plan and local regulations; no individual non-U.S. plan is material for separate disclosure.

nodes.heading: Other Postretirement Benefit Plan Assets
nodes.start_phrase: Plan assets associated with other postretirement benefits primarily represent funding of one of the U.S. postretirement benefit plans through a Voluntary Employee Beneficiary Association (“VEBA”), a tax-qualified trust.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Disclosures about other postretirement benefit plan assets and the components of net periodic benefit cost (income) for pension and other postretirement benefit plans.
- Plan funding/structure: U.S. other postretirement benefits are partially funded through a tax‑qualified VEBA trust, invested largely in liquid assets to meet near‑term benefit payments.
- Asset allocation and totals: Other postretirement plan assets totaled $419 million at December 31, 2021 ($396 million in 2020). Key classes include cash and cash equivalents, U.S. and international equities, government and corporate bonds, mutual/pooled/commingled funds, hedge funds/limited partnerships, real estate, and other assets. The largest exposures are U.S. equities, fixed income (including corporate bonds) and commingled funds, with meaningful cash holdings.
- Fair value information: Detailed fair value hierarchy levels, valuation techniques, and inputs for these assets are provided in Note 16.
- Net periodic benefit cost (income) summary (2019–2021):
  - Pension plans: Net periodic benefit income in all three years (driven by expected return on assets exceeding interest cost), partially offset by amortization of actuarial losses; after settlements, curtailments, and special termination benefits, total pension cost (income) was $(61) million in 2021, $(44) million in 2020, and $(2) million in 2019.
  - Other postretirement plans: Net periodic benefit cost in all three years, with total cost of $8 million in 2021, $24 million in 2020, and $22 million in 2019.
  - Settlement charges in pension plans were primarily tied to strategic realignment initiatives (see Note 18); curtailment effects and special termination benefits are also presented.
- Accounting policies:
  - The actual fair value of plan assets is used as the market‑related value when determining expected return on assets.
  - Actuarial gains/losses are amortized under the corridor approach (10% of the greater of the benefit obligation or market‑related value of assets), generally over the average future working lifetime of participants.
- Income statement presentation: All components except service cost are recorded in other income (loss)—net.

nodes.title: Impact on Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income
nodes.heading: Impact on Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income
nodes.start_phrase: The following table sets forth the pretax changes in AOCI for our pension and other postretirement benefit plans (in millions):
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Impact of pension and other postretirement benefit plans on Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI), showing pretax changes, year-end balances, and key actuarial and accounting assumptions.
- AOCI changes (pretax) for 2021 vs. 2020:
  - Pension plans: AOCI improved from $(3,012) million to $(2,125) million.
    - Key components in 2021: recognized prior service cost of $1 million; recognized net actuarial loss of $261 million; net actuarial gain during the year of $623 million; FX translation gain of $2 million.
  - Other postretirement plans (OPEB): AOCI improved from $(47) million to $(4) million.
    - Key components in 2021: recognized prior service credit of $2 million; recognized net actuarial loss of $3 million; net actuarial gain during the year of $27 million; prior service credit recorded during the year of $13 million; FX translation gain of $2 million.
- Notable events:
  - Recognized net actuarial losses tied to settlements related to strategic realignment initiatives: $117 million in 2021 and $23 million in 2020 (pension).
  - $15 million of 2021 net actuarial loss due to curtailments.
- Year-end AOCI composition (pretax) at December 31, 2021 vs. 2020:
  - Pension: prior service cost $(9)M (vs. $(10)M); net actuarial loss $(2,116)M (vs. $(3,002)M); total $(2,125)M (vs. $(3,012)M).
  - OPEB: prior service credit $28M (vs. $17M); net actuarial loss $(32)M (vs. $(64)M); total $(4)M (vs. $(47)M).
- Assumptions for benefit obligation measurement (12/31/2021 vs. 12/31/2020):
  - Pension: discount rate 3.00% (vs. 2.50%); interest crediting rate 3.00% (unchanged); compensation growth 3.75% (unchanged).
  - OPEB: discount rate 3.25% (vs. 2.75%).
- Assumptions for net periodic benefit cost/income (2019–2021):
  - Pension: discount rate trended down (4.00% in 2019 to 2.50% in 2021); expected long-term return on assets decreased from 7.75% (2019) to 7.25% (2021).
  - OPEB: discount rate decreased from 4.25% (2019) to 2.75% (2021); expected long-term return on assets 4.50% (2019–2020) to 4.25% (2021).
- Methodologies:
  - Discount rates determined using cash flow matching to a high-quality debt yield curve for U.S. and certain non-U.S. plans; comparable country indices for other non-U.S. plans.
  - Service and interest cost measured using spot rates along the yield curve applied to projected cash flows.
  - Compensation increase assumptions set via annual Company reviews.

nodes.title: INCOME TAXES
nodes.heading: NOTE 14: INCOME TAXES
nodes.start_phrase: Income before income taxes consisted of the following (in millions):
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 14 (Income Taxes) and Note 15 (Other Comprehensive Income) from The Coca-Cola Company’s financial statements for 2019–2021.

- Pre-tax income by geography:
  - International operations generated the majority of income before taxes: $8.9B (2021), $6.6B (2020), $7.5B (2019), versus U.S. of $3.5B, $3.1B, and $3.2B, respectively.

- Income tax expense and cash taxes:
  - Detailed current and deferred tax expense by U.S., state/local, and international jurisdictions for each year.
  - Income tax payments were $2.17B (2021), $1.27B (2020), and $2.13B (2019).

- Effective tax rate (ETR) and key drivers:
  - ETRs: 21.1% (2021), 20.3% (2020), 16.7% (2019).
  - Drivers include earnings in lower-tax foreign jurisdictions, equity method income, state taxes, and stock-based compensation.
  - Tax incentives in Brazil, Costa Rica, Singapore, and Eswatini (expiring 2023–2036, expected to be renewed) reduced income tax expense by $381M (2021), $317M (2020), and $335M (2019).
  - Discrete items impacted ETR, including changes in foreign tax laws and updates to uncertain tax positions, as well as gains on acquisitions (fairlife, BodyArmor) and other audit-related matters.

- Policy and structural tax matters:
  - GILTI: Company elected to recognize GILTI tax effects in the period incurred (no deferred recognition).
  - Indefinite reinvestment: No deferred taxes recorded on approximately $5.1B of additional outside basis differences in foreign subsidiaries.
  - Audit status: U.S. federal examinations complete for years prior to 2007; most state and foreign jurisdictions not subject to audit for years prior to 2006. Carryforwards from the CCE North America acquisition remain open until utilized.

- Uncertain tax positions (UTPs):
  - Gross unrecognized tax benefits: $906M at 12/31/2021 (vs. $915M in 2020; $392M in 2019).
  - If the Company prevails on all UTPs, the benefit would be $600M (excluding interest/penalties); remaining $306M reflects jurisdictional offsets.
  - Interest and penalties accrued: $453M (2021), $391M (2020), $201M (2019); related expense recognized: $62M (2021), $190M (2020), $11M (2019).
  - Changes expected within 12 months due to audits/settlements, but not expected to significantly impact the financial statements.
  - IRS transfer pricing litigation: Tax Court Opinion (Nov. 18, 2020) largely in IRS’s favor; Company disagrees and will vigorously defend (affected judgments on tax positions).

- Deferred taxes and carryforwards:
  - 12/31/2021: Net deferred tax liability of $0.7B, versus net deferred tax asset of $0.6B at 12/31/2020.
  - Key deferred tax assets include intangibles, equity method investments, derivatives, other liabilities, benefit plans, and NOLs; key deferred tax liabilities include PP&E, intangibles, equity method investments, and derivatives.
  - Net DTAs outside the U.S.: $0.7B (2021) and $1.4B (2020).
  - Loss carryforwards: $2.31B available; $0.85B expire within five years, remainder later.

- Valuation allowances:
  - Balances: $401M (2021), $406M (2020), $303M (2019).
  - 2021 saw a small net decrease ($5M), mainly from changes in equity investments and NOLs.
  - 2020 increased ($103M) due to equity investments and negative evidence on NOLs/FTC utilization.
  - 2019 decreased ($116M) due to positive evidence on NOL utilization and reversals related to U.S. items; partially offset by increases tied to equity investees and acquisitions.
  - Company expects to realize remaining net DTAs based on projected taxable income; reversals could reduce tax expense if future evidence supports it.

Given the significant estimation uncertainty and sensitivity to assumptions (sales volume, pricing, royalty rates, long-term growth rates, cost of capital), they tested the design and operating effectiveness of controls over the annual impairment process, including the choice of qualitative vs. quantitative tests, review of valuation models and assumptions, and determination of reporting unit carrying values. Procedures included benchmarking key inputs to third-party and industry sources, considering market transactions, assessing management’s projections against external economic and industry forecasts, performing sensitivity analyses, back-testing prior estimates, and involving valuation specialists for discounted cash flow assumptions.
